paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Peak human running speed, compared to that of other similarly sized land animals, is 'absolutely rotten', says animal locomotion expert McNeill Alexander of the University of Leeds in the UK. If Usain Bolt, Jamaican sprinter and one of the fastest 100-meter runners of all time, raced the fifty fastest animals, he would come in around 28, just ahead of the elephant. The cheetah, of course, would take the first-place gold and the prong-homed antelope the second-place silver.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Our main disadvantage, Alexander says, is the considerable size and weight of our limbs. 'We're still suffering from having evolved from apes, whose tree-swinging lifestyles require big grasping feet and plenty of muscle all the way up the leg. What would make humans faster, according to Alexander, is if we had legs like an ostrich. Ostriches run on their toes, with their ankles 'a good bit of the way up the leg', and carry almost all their leg muscle on short thighbones at the very top. They can run up to 69 kilometers an hour (kph). Human feet are also a drawback. Unlike ostriches which have smallish feet but manage to keep their balance by spreading their wings as they run, humans have evolved big, floppy feet to keep them upright. What we gain in power and balance from the oversized appendages is more than lost in the added weight and awkwardness they cause.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In fact, it's a little surprising that humans have achieved the speeds they have. And that they keep getting faster. In the 1936 Olympics, American Jesse Owens achieved a speed of 35 kph; in 2009 Bolt reached over 42 kph. But how much faster can humans get? Is there a biological limit to human speeds? For a long time running experts assumed that the ultimate limit to how fast we can run was set by the maximum force our feet can generate against the ground. In order to find a biological limit to running speed, Peter Weyland, a researcher who studies human running at Southern Methodist University in the US, subjected a group of elite runners to a series of rather complex tests. The findings of these trials suggest that runners could generate more force with each step. Based on his research, Weyland determined that humans should be biologically capable of running up to about 65 kph.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If human speed is largely a matter of how fast our muscles can activate and pull our tendons, thus pushing us off the ground, our limits can also be traced to the molecular level – what Weyland calls our 'internal gearing'. Humans have three types of muscle fibre, two 'fast-twitch' types and one 'slow-twitch'. Fast-twitch muscles, like the ones which control our eyeballs, fire quickly and are good for expending speedy, short bursts of energy. Slow-twitch muscles, like the ones that help us stand around for long periods of time, fire slowly but can work over long periods of time. The proportion of fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers in our legs varies from person to person.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: But not all fast-twitch muscles in animals are the same. For example, says Weyland, the fast-twitch muscles in hummingbirds, which beat their wings 50 times a second, are much faster than the fast-twitch muscles in elephants. And, muscle fibers that contract, really quickly use a huge amount of energy. Thus, relatively large animals like humans wouldn't have enough energy to keep a high proportion of fast-twitch muscles going for long. But especially fast larger animals take longer strides, making foot-ground contact time less critical.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: 'When people run they are essentially bouncing through the air from one leg to another', says Daniel Lieberman of Harvard University in the USA. This points to the reasons behind Bolt's achievements, because he uses longer strides and his feet remain on the ground less than his rivals. In the Beijing Olympics in 2008, Bolt's stride was measured at about 0.3 meters longer than that of the other sprinters.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: So, how can individual humans become exceptionally fast runners? The short answer, according to Weyland is 'they can't'. There is an obvious limit to the ultimate speed any individual can attain. Because our genes determine the proportion of slow and fast muscle fibers we have, we are in a sense born with our top speed already determined. Elite sprinters tend to have a higher proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibers, while long-distance runners have a higher proportion of slow-twitch. Bob Fitts, an exercise physiologist at Marquette University in the US, agrees but points out runners can get faster. Supervised practice and exercise can help with endurance, he says, and with neural adaptations – meaning that the nerves can be trained to activate the muscles faster. And, of course, frequent exercise can give you bigger muscles. But, Fitts continues, 'you're not going to switch fibers to fast fibers other than a few per cent'. In conditions of zero gravity, slow-twitch muscles do, in fact, become about 30 per cent faster. The idea that we can't do much to run faster – short of becoming astronauts – isn't likely to satisfy people forever. If muscle fibre is biologically predetermined, couldn't we just splice some of those fast-twitch fibers of hummingbirds into our bodies? Wouldn't that make us run faster? Another possibility might be the manipulation of our own existing genes to change the nature of our muscle fibers. The science already exists to make this happen. Researchers in California in 2004 caused a switch from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscles that helped laboratory mice to burn fat.

groups.title: Improving human running speed
content: Bob Fitts from Marquette University believes that runners can, in fact, increase their speed and levels of {{23}} by exercise and practice. And, they can perhaps train their {{24}} to send messages to their muscles more quickly. However, there are few practical ways today for increasing a person's maximum running speed as this is largely biologically predetermined. In conditions of greatly reduced {{25}} the slow-twitch muscles do increase their speed, but such conditions are highly impractical. Despite these problems, it has been demonstrated that modifying a person's genes is possible if nonetheless difficult. A controlled experiment using {{26}} as subjects has yielded positive results.
